title: Salvadoran Troops Strike Haitian Gang, Killing 20 in Deadly Raid – Al Jazeera Report
body:
Salvadoran forces joined Haitian police in a coordinated raid on a notorious gang stronghold on Saturday, leaving at least 20 people dead and sparking a fresh debate over the use of foreign troops in domestic security operations. The operation, which took place in the capital Port‑au‑Prince shortly before Haitian Prime Minister Ariel Henry’s scheduled visit to El Salvador, was framed by President Nayib Bukele as a decisive strike against one of Haiti’s most powerful criminal networks. Human‑rights advocates, however, have warned that the deployment of foreign soldiers raises serious concerns under international law and could exacerbate the fragile political climate in the Caribbean nation.

The joint mission targeted the “G9” alliance, a coalition of gangs that controls large swaths of the city’s informal settlements and is widely blamed for a wave of kidnappings, extortion and murder that has crippled Haiti’s already overstretched police force. According to Haitian authorities, the raid was conducted after weeks of intelligence gathering, with Salvadoran troops providing logistical support, tactical advice and, in some instances, direct combat assistance. Bukele announced that the operation resulted in the elimination of dozens of gang members and the seizure of weapons, ammunition and cash, describing it as “a necessary step to restore order and protect the Haitian people.”

The involvement of Salvadoran soldiers marks a rare instance of a Central American country intervening militarily in another nation’s internal security affairs. Bukele, who has cultivated a reputation for hard‑line crime‑fighting policies at home, has positioned the deployment as a gesture of regional solidarity, emphasizing that Haiti’s crisis threatens broader stability across the Caribbean and Central America. He also highlighted the timing of the operation, noting that it would send a strong message ahead of Prime Minister Henry’s diplomatic trip, which aims to secure additional aid and strengthen bilateral ties.

Critics argue that the raid may have violated Haiti’s sovereignty and international human‑rights standards. The United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) and several NGOs have called for transparent investigations into the casualties, insisting that any use of force must be proportionate and that victims’ families deserve accountability. Past incidents involving foreign troops in Haiti—most notably the controversial presence of United Nations peacekeepers in the early 2000s—have left a lingering distrust among local communities, who fear that external forces may prioritize political objectives over civilian protection. Moreover, the death toll, which includes several unidentified individuals, has raised questions about whether the operation adhered to due‑process guarantees enshrined in the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, to which both Haiti and El Salvador are parties.

The Haitian government, for its part, has defended the joint action as a necessary response to an escalating security vacuum. With the national police force estimated to be outnumbered by gang members by a factor of three, officials argue that external assistance is the only viable option to dismantle entrenched criminal structures. Prime Minister Henry, speaking after the raid, praised the cooperation as “a testament to regional solidarity” and pledged to pursue further collaborative efforts with neighboring countries to combat organized crime. Nonetheless, opposition parties and civil‑society groups have warned that reliance on foreign militaries could undermine the development of a capable, independent Haitian security apparatus, perpetuating a cycle of dependency.

As the aftermath of the raid unfolds, the international community will be watching closely to see how Haiti balances the urgent need for security with the imperative to uphold human rights and national sovereignty. The upcoming visit by Prime Minister Henry to El Salvador is expected to include discussions on broader security cooperation, potential financial assistance, and mechanisms for monitoring the conduct of any future joint operations. Whether this episode will mark the beginning of a new model of regional security partnership—or a contentious precedent that deepens Haiti’s internal challenges—remains to be seen. In the weeks ahead, transparent investigations into the casualties and clear guidelines for any further foreign involvement will be essential to ensure that the pursuit of safety does not come at the expense of the rule of law.
